nodes.title: The buyer organization (as modelled by the advisor)
nodes.summary: The root frame: the advisor models a single buyer organization and answers 'how can Faros help?' strictly from its approved children.
nodes.interview_question: Why model a whole 'buyer organization' as the root instead of just listing Faros features?

nodes.title: Faros AI — offering root
nodes.summary: Faros V observes AI work from tickets to outcomes to spend, optimizes context, and governs with provenance — one platform spanning the whole chain.
nodes.interview_question: In one sentence, what is Faros — and why isn't it just another FinOps or DevEx dashboard?

competitor.name: Harness
competitor.positioning: Harness pitches one end-to-end software-delivery platform too, and its AI DLC Insights (May 2026) sells the same 'token spend → shipped software' story — the closest whole-platform analog.

nodes.title: Token Intelligence — trace AI spend to outcomes
nodes.summary: Traces token consumption and classifies it productive / inefficient / wasteful, attributing spend to people, teams, and the outcomes it delivered.
nodes.interview_question: How do you actually attribute a token to an outcome, and where does that attribution become an estimate rather than a fact?

competitor.name: Harness
competitor.positioning: Harness AI DLC Insights markets the same 'see what your AI tokens shipped' join and is the #1 watch-list threat to this exact card.

nodes.title: Token Attribution Ledger — every token to its outcome
nodes.summary: The ledger that ties every dollar of AI spend to the work it produced and the outcome it shipped — the substrate under Token Intelligence.
nodes.interview_question: What's in the ledger at the row level, and what stops it from being a prettier version of a cost report?

competitor.name: Exceeds AI
competitor.positioning: Exceeds AI does commit/line-level AI-vs-human diffing and is outcome-priced (<$20K/yr) — a cheaper, narrower attack on the same attribution claim.

nodes.title: Engineering World Model — the unified graph
nodes.summary: A single source of truth connecting teams, tools, repos, and workflows — the graph that makes cross-stage attribution possible.
nodes.interview_question: You call it a 'world model' — how is that different from a service catalog or an internal developer portal?

competitor.name: Cortex
competitor.positioning: Cortex (and Port/Backstage) already claim to be the system-of-record graph of services and ownership; they argue the catalog they own is the real source of truth.

nodes.title: AI Transformation — measure and scale AI adoption with ROI
nodes.summary: Measures the productivity impact and ROI of AI coding tools with causal analysis, cohort/A-B tests, CFO-ready reports, and the GAINS maturity roadmap.
nodes.interview_question: What exactly is the 'causal analysis' here — and can you defend it without naming an estimator you haven't published?

competitor.name: Jellyfish
competitor.positioning: Jellyfish ships an 'AI Impact' report today — but openly calls it correlation, which is the contrast Faros leans on; the risk is buyers can't tell the two apart on a slide.

nodes.title: GAINS — Generative AI Impact Net Score diagnostic
nodes.summary: A diagnostic that benchmarks AI maturity, surfaces organizational friction, and ties AI usage to outcomes.
nodes.interview_question: Is GAINS a real diagnostic with a defensible scale, or a lead-gen framework? What's the n behind the benchmark?

competitor.name: DX (Atlassian)
competitor.positioning: DX (now Atlassian, ~$1B) owns the credible quant+qual DevEx benchmark with the largest research bench — the strongest incumbent on 'maturity diagnostics'.

nodes.title: Executive Scorecards — boardroom KPI & AI-impact view
nodes.summary: Engineering KPI and AI-impact monitoring packaged for leadership and the board.
nodes.interview_question: What does a CFO see here that they can't already get from Jellyfish's exec view?

competitor.name: Jellyfish
competitor.positioning: Jellyfish's entire wedge is the engineering-to-business exec dashboard with allocation and AI Impact — it's the default boardroom incumbent.

nodes.title: Developer Productivity — DORA/SPACE/DevEx analytics
nodes.summary: DORA / SPACE / DevEx dashboards, surveys, and benchmarks that identify and remove friction from developer workflows.
nodes.interview_question: This is a crowded category — why would a team rip out LinearB or Swarmia for this?

competitor.name: LinearB
competitor.positioning: LinearB, Swarmia, Jellyfish and DX all own ticket→PR→deploy analytics today; this is the most contested, least-differentiated Faros surface.

nodes.title: DORA Metrics — accurate, attributed delivery KPIs
nodes.summary: Accurate, granular, correctly-attributed DORA metrics even in messy enterprise environments.
nodes.interview_question: Everyone claims 'accurate DORA' — what makes your attribution correct where others get it wrong?

competitor.name: Swarmia
competitor.positioning: Swarmia and LinearB sell DORA dashboards as a core, mature product at a known per-dev price — commodity pressure on this node.

nodes.title: Clara — Context Engineering for AI agents
nodes.summary: Bootstraps AI coding agents with institutional knowledge from past PRs and tickets, delivers agentic PRs with a human in the loop, and learns from every merge.
nodes.interview_question: If Cursor and Copilot keep adding their own codebase context, what's left for Clara to own?

competitor.name: Cursor
competitor.positioning: Cursor/Copilot add in-IDE codebase context natively and own the session; they argue context belongs in the tool, not a separate platform.

nodes.title: Historical Replay — learn context from past PRs
nodes.summary: Derives context from past PRs and tickets and replays it until agent success rates climb.
nodes.interview_question: Is 'replay' shipped or aspirational? Show me the loop running on real history, not a demo.

competitor.name: Unblocked
competitor.positioning: Unblocked builds answers from a codebase's history and discussions; it owns the 'learn from the past' framing for individual developers.

nodes.title: Task-to-Tool / Model Routing — right model per task
nodes.summary: Identifies which tool-model pairings work best for each kind of work and recommends the right model per task type.
nodes.interview_question: Routing changes weekly as models ship — how is your recommendation anything but stale by the time it's acted on?

competitor.name: Cursor
competitor.positioning: Cursor and other IDEs already let developers pick/route models in-session; native routing undercuts an external recommendation layer.

nodes.title: Optimize — context that makes AI accurate
nodes.summary: Generates skills, rules, and tools tailored to each repo and recommends models per task — the pillar that turns observation into better agent performance.
nodes.interview_question: Which parts of Optimize are shipped today versus roadmap? Be specific about the line.

competitor.name: GitHub Copilot
competitor.positioning: Copilot/Cursor optimize in-session with their own context and rules files; the in-tool incumbent is the default 'good enough' for most teams.

nodes.title: Observe — the operational graph
nodes.summary: The shipped operational graph that joins ticket→session→PR→deploy→incident→spend at session, file, and decision grain — Faros's load-bearing pillar.
nodes.interview_question: Where does the join actually break — which edges in that chain are inferred rather than observed?

competitor.name: Backstage
competitor.positioning: Backstage/Cortex/Port/OpsLevel own the service/ownership graph and claim to be the operational source of truth — they break at measurement and AI-session attribution, but they own the 'graph' word.

nodes.title: Govern — policy, distributed context, provenance
nodes.summary: Central policy with distributed context, provenance/audit, and compensating controls (feature flags over hard blocks) — humans still review and merge.
nodes.interview_question: What in Govern is live versus roadmap, and how is a 'compensating control' more than a feature flag with a nicer name?

competitor.name: GitHub Copilot
competitor.positioning: GitHub native branch protection, rulesets, and Advanced Security already govern what merges; the platform incumbent argues governance lives in the SCM, not a layer above it.

nodes.title: Governance & Guardrails — policy, flags, code tagging
nodes.summary: Enforce governance and guardrails at scale via policy, feature flags, and code tagging.
nodes.interview_question: You marked this 'inference' — what can you actually demonstrate today versus what you're hoping to ship?

competitor.name: GitHub Copilot
competitor.positioning: GitHub Advanced Security and native policy enforcement are the established guardrail layer most enterprises already pay for.

nodes.title: Provenance & Audit Trail — ticket to shipped change
nodes.summary: Audit trails from ticket to shipped change for AI regulatory compliance.
nodes.interview_question: With the EU AI Act high-risk deadline now deferred to Dec 2027, how do you keep this from being a compliance feature looking for a deadline?

competitor.name: Datadog
competitor.positioning: Datadog (and SCM-native audit logs) already provide audit/observability trails enterprises trust; Faros must prove the AI-session-level provenance is uniquely needed.

nodes.title: Predictable Delivery — initiative tracking & forecasting
nodes.summary: Creates transparency, predictability, and consistency across cross-team initiatives via tracking, delay/overrun forecasting, and capacity analytics.
nodes.interview_question: This is a PMO/planning surface outside the Observe/Optimize/Govern thesis — does it dilute the story or extend it?

competitor.name: Jellyfish
competitor.positioning: Jellyfish and LinearB own engineering planning, allocation, and delivery forecasting as a primary product — this is their home turf, not Faros's.

nodes.title: Initiative Tracking — commitments, forecasting, portfolio
nodes.summary: Tracks initiative progress, aligns teams to priorities, and forecasts whether delivery commitments will be hit.
nodes.interview_question: How is this not just a Jira rollup with a forecast on top?

competitor.name: Jellyfish
competitor.positioning: Jellyfish's allocation and deliverable tracking is a flagship feature with years of enterprise traction.

nodes.title: Software Cost Capitalization — audit-ready, automated
nodes.summary: Generates accurate, audit-ready capitalization reports automatically — no manual spreadsheets.
nodes.interview_question: Capitalization is a finance workflow far from AI ROI — why is Faros the right vendor for the CFO's auditors?

competitor.name: Jellyfish
competitor.positioning: Jellyfish explicitly sells software capitalization to finance teams already — a direct, mature competitor on this exact node.

nodes.title: Flow — board asks 'what did the AI spend buy?'
nodes.summary: The reporting flow where Maya must answer the board on AI spend with evidence, spanning Copilot/Cursor/Claude Code spend, delivery dashboards, surveys, and a spreadsheet.
nodes.interview_question: Walk me through this flow the way Maya lives it — where exactly does today's tooling leave her without an answer?

competitor.name: CloudZero
competitor.positioning: CloudZero's survey says 87% of finance leaders need to tie AI spend to results and only 22% can — but CloudZero sells the spend side and stops at 'a chart, not a chargeback.'

nodes.title: Flow — from production incident to root cause
nodes.summary: The signature flow: a P1 incident traced back through deploy and PR to the AI session and the context it did or didn't have.
nodes.interview_question: When you say you trace an incident to the AI session that caused it — is that an observed edge or an inference at the PR/aggregate level?

competitor.name: Rootly
competitor.positioning: Rootly and incident.io tie an incident to its causing PR and resolve single incidents deeper than Faros — but they stop before the AI session and spend.

nodes.title: Mapping — Maya's board-ROI pain → Token Attribution Ledger
nodes.summary: Maps Maya's 'can't tell the board what the spend produced' to the Token Attribution Ledger that ties dollars to shipped outcomes — the 'door' card.
nodes.interview_question: This is your opening move. What's the single proof point that makes the board believe the attribution?

competitor.name: Harness
competitor.positioning: Harness AI DLC Insights targets the identical board-ROI buying moment with a 'token spend → shipped software' pitch.

nodes.title: Mapping — which AI tools/models are worth keeping → Optimize
nodes.summary: Maps 'too many tools/models — which to keep, scope, or cut' to Optimize's keep/scope/cut verdicts and per-task model recommendations.
nodes.interview_question: A keep/scope/cut verdict is a strong claim — what evidence backs a 'cut' recommendation that a VP would stake budget on?

competitor.name: Vantage
competitor.positioning: Vantage and CloudZero already give spend-rationalization verdicts on the cost side; they own 'what to cut' for FinOps but can't tie it to delivered outcomes.

nodes.title: Mapping — Maya's incident-to-cause pain → Observe
nodes.summary: Maps the 'trail goes cold at every tool boundary' pain to the Observe graph that joins the chain and reaches the one missing repo rule.
nodes.interview_question: What does 'the trail goes cold' look like in a real customer's stack, and how many boundaries does Observe actually cross unaided?

competitor.name: Rootly
competitor.positioning: Rootly/incident.io own incident→PR causation and the on-call's trust; they argue root-cause lives in the incident tool, not an analytics graph.

nodes.title: Mapping — Maya's repeat-mistakes pain → Negative Memory
nodes.summary: Maps 'agents repeat last week's mistake; lessons live in one senior's head' to replaying the failed session and writing the rule back into repo context.
nodes.interview_question: Negative memory is the most compelling story and it's roadmap — how do you sell the vision without over-promising it as shipped?

competitor.name: Unblocked
competitor.positioning: Unblocked and Pieces own developer/team memory of past context; they capture knowledge but not an org-level negative-memory governance loop.

nodes.title: Mapping — Maya's 'answer up, deliver commitments' → Predictable Delivery
nodes.summary: Maps Maya's pressure to hit and report commitments without policing the team to delivery tracking, forecasting, and capacity analytics.
nodes.interview_question: You labelled this 'inference' — what's the evidence the delivery surface actually serves Maya's pain, not just exists on the site?

competitor.name: Jellyfish
competitor.positioning: Jellyfish/LinearB are the established answer to 'predict and report delivery'; this mapping competes on their core promise.

nodes.title: Mapping — Maya's 'throughput up, rework up' → Clara Context Engine
nodes.summary: Maps 'AI shifted the bottleneck to review; bugs and rework rising faster than throughput' to Clara's review-ready, context-bootstrapped agent PRs.
nodes.interview_question: '40% less rework' — is that a Faros customer result or a marketing number? What's independent here?

competitor.name: SonarQube
competitor.positioning: SonarQube and GitClear own code-quality/churn measurement (GitClear's churn data even corroborates the problem) — they quantify rework but don't fix it at the agent-context level.

nodes.title: Mapping — Maya's 'empower the team, never rank it' → Developer Experience
nodes.summary: Maps 'help not surveillance; improve the team without ranking individuals' to DevEx that exposes variability across teams, not people.
nodes.interview_question: How do you guarantee a 'team variability' view doesn't get turned into an individual ranking by the customer's own managers?

competitor.name: DX (Atlassian)
competitor.positioning: DX (Atlassian) is the gold standard for survey-based, non-ranking DevEx measurement and would be Maya's natural first call here.

nodes.title: Mapping — Maya's 'make adoption stick & prove ROI' → AI Transformation
nodes.summary: Maps 'board wants the AI line item justified; adoption is uneven' to AI Transformation's causal ROI, cohort tests, CFO reports, and GAINS.
nodes.interview_question: What's your honest read on adoption — does Faros prove ROI, or just measure adoption and call it ROI?

competitor.name: Jellyfish
competitor.positioning: Jellyfish's AI Impact is the incumbent 'prove AI adoption ROI' report; the buyer will demand the causal-vs-correlation distinction be made obvious.

nodes.title: Mapping — 'is this surveillance?' → repo/system-level governance
nodes.summary: Maps the surveillance fear to the discipline that everything lands at repo/system level — context, flags, traces, policy — never individual keystrokes.
nodes.interview_question: What technically prevents a customer from using your data to rank or monitor individual engineers?

competitor.name: DX (Atlassian)
competitor.positioning: The anti-pattern is older developer-productivity/surveillance tooling that ranks individuals; Faros must visibly distance itself from that whole category.

nodes.title: Mapping — govern AI merges without slowing down → compensating controls
nodes.summary: Maps 'govern AI merges without killing velocity' to compensating controls — ship behind a feature flag instead of a hard block; a human still merges.
nodes.interview_question: A feature flag is a developer convention, not governance — what makes this a control a CISO would sign off on?

competitor.name: GitHub Copilot
competitor.positioning: GitHub native rulesets/required reviews are the velocity-vs-control default; the incumbent argues you don't need a third party to gate merges.

nodes.title: Maya — VP Platform Engineering (primary buyer)
nodes.summary: The primary buyer: VP Platform Eng at a ~1,200-eng B2B SaaS, ~90% AI adoption, renewal looming. Squeezed between a board demanding ROI and developers demanding no surveillance.
nodes.interview_question: Is Maya the economic buyer or the champion? Who actually signs, and who can veto?

nodes.title: Principle — empower the team, never police it
nodes.summary: Measurement and governance land at the repo/system level — never individual keystrokes. The line between a tool developers adopt and one they route around.
nodes.interview_question: This is a value, not a feature. How is 'empower not police' enforced in the product rather than just promised in the deck?

competitor.name: DX (Atlassian)
competitor.positioning: Every DevEx/productivity vendor claims 'we don't surveil'; the principle only differentiates if Faros can prove enforcement where rivals only assert intent.

nodes.title: Principle — transfer of mastery (human + machine memory)
nodes.summary: A senior's hard-won lesson becomes the team's standing knowledge — read by the next junior and by every agent. The narrative climax that closes the MIT learning gap.
nodes.interview_question: This is your emotional close. What's the one customer story where transfer-of-mastery actually happened, not just could happen?

competitor.name: Unblocked
competitor.positioning: Unblocked/Pieces sell 'capture and reuse team knowledge'; they own the personal/team memory story but not the human+agent governance loop Faros frames.
